payload.title: Add secure login to this application.

contract.goal: Implement secure login endpoints for this application, reusing the existing user model and session store
constraints: Reuse the existing SessionStore and UserRepo; do not add a database
Do not add new paid infrastructure or external services
Keep all changes covered by vitest tests under tests/auth/

acceptance_criteria.condition: A valid login credential creates a user session and GET /me returns the user
An expired login credential is rejected with HTTP 401
A login credential cannot be reused after its first successful use
Changes stay within the allowed scope
The whole test suite still passes

contract.goal: Add a minimal login page that submits an email address to the backend login endpoint and shows the result
constraints: Plain HTML and vanilla JavaScript only; no framework, no build step; create the public/ directory if it does not exist
The page must call POST /auth/request with a JSON body {"email": "..."} and display the response message

acceptance_criteria.condition: public/login.html exists and contains a form posting an email to /auth/request
Changes stay within the allowed scope

questions.text: Which login mechanism? (a) Passwordless magic link: user posts their email, the app emails a one-time token via the existing EmailSender, the token is exchanged for a session. (b) Passwordless one-time code: same as (a) but a short numeric code is emailed and posted back together with the email. (c) Email + password: requires adding a password hash to the user model/seed data (there is none today) and a hashing library. My recommendation is (a) because it matches the inputs and criteria with no model changes.

Endpoint names and shapes. Proposed: POST /auth/login with JSON {"email"} -> 202 {"ok":true}; POST /auth/verify with JSON {"token"} -> 200 {"user"} and starts the session; POST /auth/logout -> 204. Alternatives: GET /auth/verify?token=... (link-click style), or different path prefixes such as /login and /login/verify. Should I go with the proposal, or do you want specific paths/payloads?

How should the session be delivered to the client? (a) HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Secure cookie named "session", read by GET /me (recommended for browser clients). (b) Session id returned in the verify JSON body and sent back as Authorization: Bearer <id> (simpler for API clients). (c) Both accepted.
Lifetimes: proposed login-token expiry 15 minutes and session TTL 24 hours, both overridable via createApp options and driven by an injected clock in tests. Accept these defaults or specify others?

Behavior when POST /auth/login is called with an email that has no user: (a) still return 202 {"ok":true} and send nothing, to avoid account enumeration (recommended); (b) return 404. Also, should invalid, expired, and already-used tokens all produce the same 401 {"error":"invalid or expired login token"} response, or do you want distinct error messages per case?

Storage for pending login tokens: I plan a new in-memory LoginTokenStore under src/auth/ (single-use, expiring, injected clock), keyed by a random 32-byte token, alongside the reused SessionStore for sessions. Tokens would be looked up by hash of the token value so the raw secret is never stored. Is that acceptable, or do you prefer a different approach (for example reusing SessionStore for tokens)?
Is a POST /auth/logout endpoint (revokes the session via SessionStore.revoke) in scope, or should I omit it to keep the change minimal?

response.reason: The goal says "secure login" but does not name the mechanism. The existing User model has no password field, the inputs include the MemoryEmailSender, and the acceptance criteria talk about a credential that expires and cannot be reused, which points at an emailed one-time link/code, but that is an inference. Choosing the mechanism, endpoint shapes, and lifetimes myself would change the implementation materially, so I am asking first.

questions.text: What response format should the login page display from POST /auth/request? Options: (A) JSON object with a `message` string, (B) plain-text response body, or (C) support both by preferring JSON `message` and falling back to response text. This materially changes response parsing and error handling.

answers.answer: (a) passwordless magic link via the existing EmailSender; tokens expire after 15 minutes and are single-use; no passwords.

Use POST /auth/request (not /auth/login) with JSON {email} -> 202 {status:'sent', message:'Check your email for a login link'}; POST /auth/verify {token} -> 200 {user} and starts the session; POST /auth/logout -> 204; GET /me -> user or 401. The frontend posts to /auth/request and shows the message field.
(a) HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie named session; Secure only in production.
(a) return 202 and send nothing for unknown emails; a new request invalidates earlier unredeemed tokens for that email.
Accept the in-memory LoginTokenStore under src/auth/, storing SHA-256 hashes of the token.

interpretation: Create a minimal standalone `public/login.html` using only semantic HTML, basic CSS, and vanilla JavaScript.
Submit the entered email with `fetch` as POST `/auth/request`, using JSON `{ "email": "..." }` and the `Content-Type: application/json` header.
Display JSON `message` when available, otherwise raw response text; preserve backend messages for non-2xx responses and show a readable message for network failures.
assumptions: The page is served from the same origin as the backend endpoint, so `/auth/request` needs no CORS or base-URL configuration.
Native `type="email"` and `required` validation are sufficient for this minimal page.
A single status region can show pending, success, backend-error, and network-error states.
risks: A malformed JSON response declaring JSON content type must still fall back safely to its raw response body.
Repeated submissions should not overlap or leave the submit control disabled after a failure.

verification_plan.AC-1: Run the exact contract command: `grep -q '/auth/request' public/login.html && grep -qi 'type="email"' public/login.html`; additionally inspect the form script for POST, JSON headers/body, and result rendering.
verification_plan.AC-2: Run `git status --short` and `git diff --name-only` to confirm every changed/untracked path is under `public/**` or `tests/ui/**`.

payload.message: Contract v2 accepted after response-format clarification; implementation work has started.

interpretation: Add passwordless magic-link login: POST /auth/request takes {email}, always answers 202 {status:'sent', message:'Check your email for a login link'}, and for known users emails a one-time token through the existing EmailSender; unknown emails get the same 202 and no email.

POST /auth/verify takes {token}; a live, unused token creates a session in the existing SessionStore (24h TTL), sets an HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie named session (Secure only when NODE_ENV=production), and returns 200 {user}. Expired, unknown, or already-used tokens return 401.

Tokens are 32 random bytes, expire after 15 minutes, are stored only as SHA-256 hashes in a new in-memory LoginTokenStore under src/auth/, are consumed on first successful verify, and a new request for the same email invalidates that email's earlier unredeemed tokens.
GET /me reads the session cookie and returns the user (200) or 401 {error:'not authenticated'}; POST /auth/logout revokes the session, clears the cookie and returns 204.

createApp keeps its default of new UserRepo() so existing tests still pass, and additionally accepts sessions, email sender, clock and lifetimes so tests can inject a deterministic clock and read tokens from MemoryEmailSender.sent.
All new tests live under tests/auth/, including the two files named by the acceptance checks; edits are limited to src/auth/**, src/app.ts and tests/auth/**.
assumptions: Tests obtain the token by parsing the login link from MemoryEmailSender.sent, so the email text contains the raw token in a URL like /auth/verify?token=<token>; the actual verify happens via POST /auth/verify {token}.
'Production' for the cookie Secure flag means NODE_ENV === 'production', resolved at request time so tests can exercise both branches.
Error responses use the existing JSON shape {error: string}; invalid, expired and used tokens share one 401 message to avoid leaking token state.
Request body validation uses zod, which is already a dependency; malformed bodies return 400.
No new npm dependencies are added; hashing and randomness come from node:crypto / WebCrypto.
risks: Existing tests/app.test.ts asserts GET /me returns 401 {error:'not authenticated'} with no cookie; the new implementation must preserve that exact body.

The reused SessionStore uses Date.now by default; unless the same injected clock is passed to both the token store and the session store, expiry tests could be non-deterministic. I will wire one clock through createApp.
Hono's cookie helpers set Secure automatically in some modes; I will set attributes explicitly to match the spec.
AC-3 is human-reviewed; I will add an explicit reuse test (second verify with the same token returns 401 and creates no second session) so the reviewer has direct evidence.

verification_plan.AC-1: tests/auth/valid-login.test.ts: POST /auth/request for a seeded email, read the token from MemoryEmailSender.sent, POST /auth/verify, assert 200 {user}, a Set-Cookie header with session=..., HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax, then GET /me with that cookie returns 200 and the same user. Run with npx vitest run tests/auth/valid-login.test.ts and confirm it passes.
verification_plan.AC-2: tests/auth/expired-login.test.ts: request a token, advance the injected clock past 15 minutes, POST /auth/verify, assert status 401 and no Set-Cookie; also assert a token one millisecond before expiry still works so the boundary is pinned. Run with npx vitest run tests/auth/expired-login.test.ts and confirm it passes.
verification_plan.AC-3: tests/auth/reuse-login.test.ts: verify a token successfully, then verify the same token again and assert 401 with no new cookie, and that a new /auth/request invalidates the earlier token. Run it and include the output in the evidence summary for the human reviewer.
verification_plan.AC-4: Before submitting, run git status --porcelain and git diff --stat against the base commit and confirm every changed path matches src/auth/**, src/app.ts or tests/auth/**.
verification_plan.AC-5: Run npx vitest run for the full suite and npx tsc --noEmit, and confirm both exit 0 with all pre-existing tests still green.

AC-2.note: npx vitest run tests/auth/expired-login.test.ts: 3/3 passed. Clock advanced 15min+1ms -> POST /auth/verify returns 401 {error:'invalid or expired login token'} with no Set-Cookie; exactly 15min still accepted; unknown token -> 401.

AC-3.note: Human review. Evidence: tests/auth/reuse-login.test.ts (2/2 passed) shows second verify with the same token -> 401 and no cookie, and a new /auth/request invalidates the earlier token. Mechanism: LoginTokenStore.consume() deletes the hash record before checking expiry (src/auth/token-store.ts), so a token can never be redeemed twice; only SHA-256 hashes are stored.

submission.summary: Passwordless magic-link login per contract v2. POST /auth/request {email} -> 202 {status:'sent', message:'Check your email for a login link'} for known and unknown emails alike; known users get an email via the existing EmailSender containing /auth/verify?token=<32 random bytes, base64url>. POST /auth/verify {token} consumes the token (single-use, 15 min TTL, stored only as SHA-256 hash in new in-memory LoginTokenStore under src/auth/), creates a 24h session in the reused SessionStore, sets HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie 'session' (Secure when NODE_ENV=production or isProduction option), returns 200 {user}. POST /auth/logout revokes and clears the cookie -> 204. GET /me returns {user} or 401 {error:'not authenticated'} (existing test body preserved). Malformed bodies -> 400. createApp(users, options) keeps backward compatibility and accepts sessions/email/now/ttls/isProduction/baseUrl for deterministic tests. Committed as 5dd6d44 on relay/t-backend-auth.
